newsitem.title: GERMANY: Suspected neo-Nazis burn down Luebeck church.
newsitem.headline: Suspected neo-Nazis burn down Luebeck church.

text.p: Suspected neo-Nazi arsonists scrawled swastikas on the brick facade of a Catholic church before burning it down in the north German port of Luebeck early on Sunday, police said.

Firefighters found five Nazi swastika symbols sprayed in white paint on the St Vicelin Church alongside the name of a local priest who is campaigning to stop Algerian asylum-seekers from being deported, police said.
The fire started in a shed next to the church. Several bottles of propane gas in the shed exploded, spreading the blaze to the church, firefighters said. No one was injured.
The building was too dangerous to enter and firefighters said the fire would probably have to be left to burn out.
Police suspected extreme right-wingers and prosecutors were treating the fire as aggravated arson.

German left-wing and anti-racist groups condemned the arson attack, recalling two fires in a synagogue in the city in 1994 and 1995. Police said the first was a racist attack and the second was never cleared up.

Father Guenther Harig, whose name was scrawled on the church, works in another Luebeck parish and gave refuge to a family of asylum-seekers inside his church after authorities refused them political asylum at the beginning of May.

Luebeck mayor Michael Bouteiller told journalists the city's efforts to protect the rights of foreigners were a "provocation" to Luebeck's exteme right wing, which he said was no bigger than anywhere else in Germany.

In January last year 10 foreigners, most of them asylum-seekers from Africa, died in a hostel fire in Luebeck, sparking fears of a new wave of neo-Nazi violence similar to one that swept the country after unification in 1990.
Police initially detained right-wing youths but released them. A Lebanese resident, Safwan Eid, was charged with arson and is now on trial.
